entries.when: Your best guess — you think it's likely (~70%+). tabun ame da (It's probably rain). Everyday default.
Opens a question or surprise — "Could it be that…?" moshikashite kare? (Could it be him?). You might be wrong.
Uncertainty on a statement — ame kamoshirenai (It might rain). Attach to verb/adj; not a standalone question word. Use for "might", not casual "maybe" (that's tabun).
Standalone pronoun — one thing near you. kore wa nan? (What is this?). Never put a noun after it.
Must sit before a noun — kono hon (this book). For plural: kono hon-tachi ≈ "these books."
Standalone plural near you — korera wa hon (These are books). Points at several items, not modifying a noun.
Standalone — near the listener or just mentioned. sore kudasai (Give me that).
Before a noun — sono mise (that shop). Same "so" distance as sore.
Standalone plural — sorera wa furui (Those are old).
Near the speaker — where you are standing.
Near the listener — where they are or what you just pointed at.
Away from both of you — across the room or down the street.
Question word — doko? (Where?). Same ko/so/a/do pattern.
Broad verb — listen, hear, or ask. ongaku wo kiku (listen to music), namae wo kiku (ask a name). Default everyday "ask."
Deliberate inquiry — michi wo tazuneru (ask for directions). More formal/focused; not for "listen to music."
Depart a place — koko wo saru (leave here). Literary/formal feel; person or thing moves away.
Exit outward — ie wo deru (leave the house), dekakeru (go out). Physical "go out of" somewhere.
Leave something for someone — nimotsu wo nokosu (leave luggage behind). Object stays; you go.
Quit a job, school, or habit — kaisha wo yameru (quit the company). Not physical departure.
The rest, apart from what was mentioned — hoka ni nanika? (Anything else?). hoka no hito (other people). Most common "other."
Emphasizes separation — betsu no houhou (a different method), betsubetsu ni (separately). "Different" more than "the rest."
Catch-all for leftovers in lists — ringo, banana, sonota (apples, bananas, and others). Formal "etc."
Counting/addition — "one more." mou hitotsu kudasai (One more, please). Specific quantity, not "other" in general.
The action — to work. kaisha de hataraku (work at a company). Verb: what you do.
The job itself — shigoto ga aru (I have work). Noun: the thing/place/task.
Polite default — bumping someone, getting attention, apologizing, or thanking for a favor.
Friends/family only — quick sorry. Stepped on a toe, late to meet up.
Casual-masculine sorry between close peers. Slightly weightier than gomen.
Quantity or degree — motto tabetai (want to eat more), motto ookii (bigger). "More of" something.
Adding to a point — sarani mondai ga aru (Furthermore, there's a problem). Formal "in addition" in speech/writing.
"Again" — mata kite (Come again). Can mean "also" in lists, but primary sense is repetition.
Particle on a noun — watashi mo iku (I'm going too). "In addition" attached to the thing.
Hasn't happened yet — mada tabetenai (haven't eaten yet). Or "still" continuing.
Already done — mou tabeta (already ate). With negative: mou ikanai (not going anymore).
Polite default — okaasan wa doko? (Where is mother?). Respectful, any age. Also accepts mum / mom.
Casual, affectionate — kids say mama. Also used by adults talking to their own kids about "mom."
Polite default — otousan wa kaisha desu (Dad is at work). Also accepts father.
Casual, childish — papa! Same vibe as English "daddy."
Everyday word for your job — shigoto ga aru (I have work).
Loanword — business world, deals, commerce. Not "my shift today" (that's shigoto).
Broad — a problem, issue, or test question. mondai nai (no problem).
Personal trouble weighing on you — nayami ga aru (I have worries). More emotional than mondai.
Verb/adj — you're stuck or troubled. komatta (I'm in trouble). Action/feeling, not a noun issue.
Same word — dareka iru? (Is someone there?). Context (question vs statement) carries "any-" vs "some-."
Emphasis on "any" — daredemo dekiru (anyone can do it). Broader than dareka.
Medical doctor — isha ni iku (go to the doctor).
Honorific title — Tanaka-sensei. Used for doctors, teachers, pros. Not the word "doctor" alone.
Same word in Japanese — ureshii! covers both "I'm happy" and "I'm glad." Context decides nuance.
Enjoyable — tanoshii desu ne (That was fun). Activity feels good.
Amusing or intriguing — omoshiroi! (That's funny / interesting). Not "fun activity" (tanoshii).
Verb — something finishes. shigoto ga owaru (work finishes).
Noun — the end point. owari da (That's the end). Not the action of finishing.
Truth/reality — hontou? (Really?). Adverb or noun.
Adverb form — hontouni sou da (It's truly so). Emphasizes truth.
The truth as a fact — shinjitsu wo shitteiru (know the truth). Heavier than casual hontou.
